source.title: Beyond Performance Plateaus: A Comprehensive Study on Scalability in Speech Enhancement
source.authors: Wang-You Zhang; Kohei Saijo; Jee-weon Jung; Chen-Da Li; Shinji Watanabe; Yan-Min Qian

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present. Some table and figure content is flattened, and most plotted results have no numerical values in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in speech enhancement and reports departures from simple monotonic scaling, including an initial degradation, convergence at higher model complexity, and degraded performance with imbalanced data.
record.gate_note: The paper tests speech-enhancement performance scaling, not held-out language-model cross-entropy or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Several results are described in prose but their plotted numerical values are not supplied. Configuration tables and cited results are not treated as outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps model complexity (MACs) and data size for speech-enhancement models, a new modality, and reports how quality metrics scale. It fits no power law and measures no loss, so it bears only loosely on V5's claim that the scaling form carries over. It reports performance roughly linear in log-MACs, which then plateaus.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that scaling complexity together with multi-domain data improves SE, but gains plateau and need more data. They report double descent on the small corpus and degradation from imbalanced simulated data. They conclude that RNN-based architectures scale inefficiently and that larger multi-domain SE corpora are needed.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales speech-enhancement models and measures speech-quality, intelligibility, distortion, and downstream ASR metrics; it does not fit language-model held-out cross-entropy power laws or optimize parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with causal versus non-causal setup, training-data size and balance, model architecture, model complexity, and compute budget. GPU type also differs for TF-GridNet versus the other architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Across SE architectures, parameter count shows no clear correlation with performance; MACs is the more informative axis. Architecture choice strongly changes the scaling curve (BSRNN best at low complexity, TF-GridNet at high).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In speech enhancement, architecture changes performance substantially at matched size, and parameter count is a poor scaling variable across architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream ASR word accuracy on enhanced speech improves with SE model complexity but stays below the no-enhancement baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger front-end SE models give better downstream ASR accuracy, yet still underperform skipping enhancement.

record.problems: The text supplies few numerical outcome values beyond qualitative descriptions of plots; most scaling results are figure-based. The study does not fit power-law exponents or test language-model loss or compute-optimal allocation. The authors note limited exploration above 100 M parameters. Compute comparisons use different GPU types for TF-GridNet and other models.
record.rows_left_out: No reported outcome rows omitted. Model configuration tables and cited results were not extracted as outcomes.

untested.parts: No power-law fit, and no loss measured. Image, video, repeated-data and fine-tuning regimes are not tested.
No exponents are fitted and no fitting methods are compared.

missing.what: Non-causal models consistently outperform causal ones, and the gap widens with 157 h of data.
Models trained on 157 h gain more from added complexity than models trained on less data, an interaction of data and size.

record.verdict_notes: Speech enhancement measured by quality metrics rather than loss, with no power-law fits. The bearing on V5 is therefore weak, and V7 is not tested. Most values are figure-only. Compute comparisons use different GPUs for TF-GridNet and the other models.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute, and its scaling with compute.
Whether architecture details change language-model loss only slightly at fixed parameter count.
The study examines speech-enhancement performance, not held-out pretraining loss; it does not test image/video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study reports ASR word accuracy after speech enhancement, but does not test language-model downstream tasks or predictability from pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal split, or direct comparison of fitting methods is reported; the study does report setup-dependent scaling trends and curves that converge or regress.

rows.operation_detail: Varied model complexity and measured the reported metric group.

conditions.value: sufficient data; includes the 157 h scale

rows.measure: PESQ-WB, STOI, SDR, DNSMOS, and WAcc (reported as a shared trend)
rows.value: Increasing complexity generally improves all metrics when sufficient training data are available; the initially linear performance relationship with log-scale MACs tends to converge after complexity reaches a threshold.
rows.note: The prose describes similar trends for causal and non-causal setups; the text does not give the threshold value for this setup.
rows.check: V7 link removed. Performance is linear in log-MACs, then converges past a threshold; the authors attribute this to a data bottleneck.

rows.value: Increasing complexity generally improves all metrics when sufficient training data are available; the initially linear performance relationship with log-scale MACs tends to converge after complexity reaches a threshold.
rows.note: The authors state that the scaling effect seen at lower complexity does not hold when complexity is increased further and that more training data are needed for further scaling.

rows.subject: BSRNN
rows.operation_detail: Varied training dataset size and measured performance.

conditions.value: SDR and WAcc shown; text says all metrics improve

rows.value: All metrics keep improving monotonically with more training data; larger models tend to benefit more from increased data.
rows.note: The text gives the trend for all metrics; Figure 2 displays SDR and WAcc.
rows.check: Only three data scales and no fitted form. Improvement is monotonic, but a power-law shape cannot be shown. V7 link removed.

rows.subject: BSRNN

rows.check: The data distribution changes (93% DNS-2020), so this is not pure data scaling from the same source mix. V7 link removed.

conditions.value: OWSM v3.1 ASR; results averaged across test corpora unless specified

rows.baseline: ASR performance without speech enhancement (no processing)
rows.value: More complex models tend to achieve better WAcc, but they still underperform the no-processing baseline.
rows.note: The paper reports a directional trend but does not report a predictive fit for downstream performance.
rows.check: ASR accuracy after enhancement is not downstream performance of the scaled model itself. Recorded under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: BSRNN complexity sweeps (causal and non-causal) at 8.8 h and 157 h
relationships.reason: SE metrics rise roughly linearly in log-MACs, then plateau past a threshold (R7, R8). At 8.8 h they first degrade (double descent; R1–R6). No power-law fit is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Enhancement metrics rose roughly linearly with log-MACs before plateauing, with initial degradation at 8.8 hours.

relationships.condition: Non-causal BSRNN data scaling: 8.8, 98.8 and 157 h, then about 900 h of imbalanced simulated data
relationships.reason: Metrics improve monotonically over three data scales (R9). Adding imbalanced simulated DNS data up to about 900 h degrades performance (R10).
relationships.display_finding: Metrics improved across the initial three data scales, but adding imbalanced simulated data to about 900 hours degraded performance.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: BSRNN at 8.8 h and at higher complexity; approximately 900 h with the stated imbalanced data mix
reader_labels.reason: The reported initial metric degradation, convergence of the complexity trend, and regression after adding imbalanced data qualify the claim that the same scaling form holds across settings (R1–R10).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The study reports non-monotonic behavior on the smallest dataset, convergence at higher complexity, and degraded performance with imbalanced data, consistent with scaling curves bending across conditions (R1–R10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Word accuracy tends to improve with complexity, but the enhanced outputs remain below the no-processing baseline; the study does not establish a predictive fit (R15).
